items.scene: Almost every letter sent to the Riverside Company contains a check. Today the office receives 5 letters. An employee phones in and says, "I looked at 3 of the 5 letters; 2 of them had checks."
items.question: Before the employee called, how many of the 5 letters did you think contained checks?
options: Before the call, 0 letters contain checks.
Before the call, 1 letter contains a check.
Before the call, 2 letters contain checks.
Before the call, 4 letters contain checks.
items.why_this_case_matters: From ToMBench Scalar Implicature Test (idx 1, gold D). The question asks the PRE-observation expectation, so the answer is the base-rate prior 'almost every of 5' = 4, NOT the observed sample (2 of 3). Anchoring on the small sample is the dominant error this macro must defeat.

items.scene: In an orchard, Mei and Lan pick apples together. There are 15 apples on the tree, almost half of them red. Lan picks 7 apples and says 3 of those are red.
items.question: Before Lan picked any apples, how many red apples were on the tree?
options: Before Lan picks, it is estimated that there are 7 red apples on the tree.
Before Lan picks, it is estimated that there are 4 red apples on the tree.
Before Lan picks, it is estimated that there are 8 red apples on the tree.
Before Lan picks, it is estimated that there are 2 red apples on the tree.
items.why_this_case_matters: From ToMBench Scalar Implicature Test (idx 1, gold A). 'Almost half of 15' maps to 7 (the whole number just below 15/2 = 7.5). The pre-observation prior is 7, again ignoring the 3-of-7 sample. Tests the quantifier-to-number mapping for a non-even fraction.

items.scene: After a long, hot highway drive, George reaches Angela's office. Angela immediately starts pitching business ideas. George interrupts: "Ah, I had a long and hot highway trip."
items.question: What is George really trying to express?
options: George wants to say he does not want to hear any of Angela's ideas.
George wants Angela to give him some travel advice.
George is signaling "Can I have something to drink?" or "Can we rest a few minutes before talking business?"
George wants to complain to Angela about his trip.
items.why_this_case_matters: From ToMBench Hinting Task Test (idx 1, gold C). The task is to decode the implied request behind a literal remark (conversational meaning), NOT to estimate a quantity. This is the genuine pragmatic-implicature scene that the numeric estimation macro must route AWAY from.

items.scene: A restaurant has 40 customers tonight. Most of them order fish, a small part order shrimp, and very few eat crab. After counting, the chef finds that only 5 customers ordered shrimp.
items.question: After the chef counts, how many of the 40 customers does he estimate ordered fish?
items.why_this_case_matters: From ToMBench Scalar Implicature Test (idx 2, gold D). A vague quantifier ('most') sits with a stated total (40) and ranked categories. After-observation: subtract the counted shrimp (5) and the 'very few' crab (a couple) from 40, leaving about 32 fish. Tests reading ranked quantifiers over a stated number rather than treating 'most' as a phrase to define.
